safety: Grass only — wet pavement plus limbo is a fall waiting to happen. Shade and water breaks between rounds on hot days.

name: Capture the Flag Basics
tagline: Two teams, two flags, one field — the summer-camp classic, simplified.

materials.item: cones for the center line and jail zones

setup: Split the field with cones, mark a jail box on each side, and plant each flag where it is visible but not trivial. Two even teams.
steps: Each team hides nothing — flags stay visible from the center line at all times.
Cross into enemy territory to grab their flag; get tagged and you sit in jail.
A teammate can free you with a hand-tag — both of you get a free walk back to your side.
First team to carry the enemy flag across the center line wins the round.
Best of three rounds, then the MVPs pick the next game's teams.

variations.easier: Smaller field, flags on poles (no hiding), and jail is a 30-second time-out instead of waiting.
variations.harder: Night-vision round at dusk with glow bracelets for team colors.

safety: Set hard boundaries before starting — roads and parking lots are out of bounds, no exceptions. Sunscreen, shade, and water breaks; call the game at the first sign of heat exhaustion.

name: Flashlight Tag
tagline: Tag by flashlight beam on a summer evening — freeze when the light finds you.

materials.item: one flashlight per 4 kids (it holds one)

setup: Play at dusk in a familiar, enclosed yard — no woods, no streets. Bound it tight with cones. One flashlight for it, glow bracelet so everyone can see them.
steps: It counts to 30 with eyes closed while everyone hides within bounds.
It sweeps the flashlight beam — anyone the beam touches freezes in place.
Frozen players can be unfrozen by a free player tagging their shadow (no beam needed, just a hand tag).
Round ends when everyone is frozen or the whistle blows at 10 minutes.
New it: the first player frozen becomes it next round.

variations.easier: Daylight version: tag by pointing, no hiding — just the beam-freeze rule.
variations.harder: Two flashlights, two its, and frozen players become 'lighthouses' who can freeze others with finger-beams.

safety: Stay inside the coned boundary — no hiding near roads, water, or parking lots. An adult holds the boundary line the whole game.

name: Chalk Obstacle Course
tagline: Draw the course, then run it: hop, spin, crab-walk, and freeze between stations.
setup: Find a stretch of pavement and sketch the course first: stations every 10 feet or so, arrows between them.
steps: Station ideas: hopscotch squares, a spin circle ('spin 3 times'), crab-walk lane, balance line, jumping jacks box, freeze square.
Kids run the course in order, doing each station's move before advancing.
Time the runs — then let kids redesign one station and run it again.
Team relay: each runner does two stations, then tags the next.
Championship: the course design contest — best new station gets added permanently.

variations.easier: Four stations max, all walking-speed, with picture labels.
variations.harder: Blindfold-guide round: one partner calls directions through the course while the other (eyes open, promise) follows exactly.

safety: Chalk dust is slippery when thick — sweep the lane between runs. Hats and water on hot pavement days.

name: Frisbee Golf Nine
tagline: Nine chalk-and-cone 'holes' around the field — fewest throws wins.

materials.item: frisbees or foam discs (1 per 2 kids)

setup: Set 9 holes around the field — cones, buckets, or chalk circles — each with a tee marker 20 to 40 feet back. Number them with chalk.
steps: Groups of 2 to 4 start at different holes to avoid traffic jams.
Throw from the tee; wherever the disc lands, that's your next lie.
Hole is finished when the disc lands inside the target circle.
Count every throw. Lowest total after 9 holes wins.
Award ceremony: longest throw, best recovery, most creative throwing style.

variations.easier: Five holes, closer tees, and buckets instead of circles — bigger targets.
variations.harder: Trick-shot hole: one hole must be played between the legs or behind the back.

safety: Foam discs only near groups — never throw toward another hole's players. Call 'fore!' (or just 'heads up!') on wild throws.

name: Nature Color Scavenger
tagline: Find something in nature for every color of the rainbow — no picking allowed.

materials.item: paper color cards or a printed rainbow strip per team

setup: Make color cards (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, brown, gray). Set the search boundary — the yard, the garden beds, the nature strip.
steps: Teams get a color card set and 15 minutes on the clock.
Find something in nature matching each color — a fallen leaf, a pebble, a petal already on the ground.
Nothing gets picked, pulled, or dug up: fallen and found only.
Back at base, each team lays out its rainbow and tells the story of the hardest color.
Bonus point for the weirdest natural object that still counts as a color.

variations.easier: Four colors instead of eight, and the teacher pre-hides painted rocks as guaranteed finds.
variations.harder: Texture round: find something smooth, rough, bumpy, and soft — then rank them by touch alone, blindfolded.

safety: Look with eyes first near bushes and logs — check for bees and thorns before reaching. Wash hands after handling soil and found objects.

name: Friendship Bracelet Basics
tagline: The camp classic: knotted embroidery floss bracelets, learned in one sitting.

materials.item: pillows or clipboards to pin to

setup: Cut floss into arm-length strands (3 per bracelet). Knot the tops together and pin them to pillows — one workstation per kid.
steps: Pick 3 colors and knot them together at the top.
Learn the only knot that matters: the forward knot — make a '4' with the working thread, pull the tail through, slide it up. Twice per knot.
Work left to right, one color at a time, until the bracelet fits around a wrist.
Tie the end in a knot, braid the tails, and gift it — bracelets are for giving.
Trade-up round: everyone makes one for the person on their left.

variations.easier: Two colors, chunky yarn instead of floss, and the teacher ties the starting knot.
variations.harder: Pattern challenge: stripes, chevrons, then the diamond — photograph each stage for the camp board.

safety: Safety pins pin to pillows or denim, never to skin. Scissors cut away from fingers.

name: Sun Print Cards
tagline: Lay objects on sun-sensitive paper, let the sun do the printing.

materials.item: flat interesting objects: leaves, keys, lace, coins

setup: Keep the sunprint paper in its black bag until the last second — it exposes fast. Set up a water rinse tray in the shade.
steps: In the shade, arrange flat objects on the blue side of the paper.
Carry it into full sun and wait 3 to 5 minutes — the paper darkens around the objects.
Rinse the paper in the water tray for one minute: the background turns deep blue, the shapes stay white.
Lay flat to dry, then mount on cardstock for a finished card.
Experiment round: half the exposure time, double it — compare the three blues.

variations.easier: The teacher handles the paper; kids only arrange objects and carry with two hands.
variations.harder: Negative-space art: spell a name in objects and print the whole word in one exposure.

safety: Don't stare at the sun while timing exposures — use a timer and look away. Rinse water only, no chemicals to handle.

name: Pinwheel Garden
tagline: Paper pinwheels on sticks — then plant the whole spinning garden.
setup: Pre-cut 6-inch squares for little ones. Push the pins through pencil erasers ahead of time so no one is forcing them.
steps: Fold the square corner to corner both ways and unfold — find the center.
Cut along each fold from the corner toward the center, stopping a thumb's width short.
Fold every other point into the center and pin through all layers into the pencil eraser.
Tape the pencil to a straw for height.
Plant the garden: stick them in the ground along the walkway and watch the wind do the work.

variations.easier: The teacher does all cutting and pinning; kids decorate and plant.
variations.harder: Two-tone pinwheels: glue two contrasting squares back to back before cutting.

safety: Pushpins are teacher-handled — pinched fingers, not pierced ones. Blow, don't run with the pinwheel.

name: Sand Art Bottles
tagline: Layered colored sand in clear bottles — desert landscapes you can shake.
setup: Pour each sand color into its own tray with a funnel. One bottle per kid, caps off, trays under everything — sand travels.
steps: Pick your first color and funnel in one inch of sand.
Tilt the bottle and pour the next color against the side — layers stay cleaner on a tilt.
Alternate colors and thicknesses: thin stripes, thick bands, a mountain layer.
Top it off to the very brim so the layers can't shift, then cap it tight.
Name your landscape and shelve it where the light hits — do not shake (or do, once, to learn why not).

variations.easier: Three colors max, wide-mouth bottles, and the teacher pours while the kid picks colors.
variations.harder: Pattern challenge: symmetrical layers mirrored top to bottom.

safety: Sand stays in the trays — no throwing, no rubbing eyes. Shake hands clean before touching faces.

name: Ice Excavation Dig
tagline: Tiny toys frozen in a block of ice — excavate them with salt and droppers.
setup: Freeze the night before: toys in water-filled containers, frozen solid. One block per pair, each on a tray with towels underneath.
steps: Pop each block out and set the excavation challenge: free every toy.
Tools allowed: salt shakers, water droppers, and patience. No hammers, no teeth.
Sprinkle salt on the ice, wait 30 seconds, then drip warm water on the salty spots — watch the tunnels form.
First pair to free all their toys calls 'excavation complete'.
Science talk: why did the salt spots melt first? Test it — one cube with salt, one without, race them.

variations.easier: Crushed-ice cups instead of solid blocks: toys half-buried, dig with spoons.
variations.harder: Timed paleontology: photograph each freed toy like a museum specimen and label the 'strata' it came from.

safety: Meltwater goes in trays, not on the floor — wet floors, wet socks, slipped kids. Towels down before blocks come out.

name: Fan Boat Races
tagline: Paper boats race across a tub — powered by nothing but fanned air.

materials.item: a long shallow tub or storage bin
hand fans or stiff paper fans

setup: Fill the tub a few inches deep and tape two lane lines. Fold one demo boat slowly so everyone sees the steps; stack paper for the fleet.
steps: Everyone folds a classic paper boat — teacher demos, kids follow.
Float-test: set boats in the tub. Leakers get 2 minutes of repairs.
Racers stand at one end with fans. On 'go', fan your boat down the lane — no touching the boat, no blowing with mouths.
First boat to cross the far tape wins the heat; winners race winners.
Redesign round: fold a wider, narrower, or double-hull boat and re-race.

variations.easier: Pre-folded boats; kids decorate and fan only.
variations.harder: Storm round: everyone fans at once from both ends — last boat floating upright wins.

safety: Towels around the tub before racing starts — splashes happen. Paper cuts: fold slowly, crease with a ruler edge.

name: Indoor Campfire Circle
tagline: Build a paper campfire, kill the lights, and tell stories around it.

materials.item: brown paper bags or construction paper
a battery tea light or flashlight
stones or gray paper for the ring

setup: Tear or cut brown paper into log shapes. Cut tissue into flame shapes. Arrange seating in a tight circle before building.
steps: Build the fire ring: gray paper stones in a circle on the floor.
Crisscross the paper logs teepee-style inside the ring.
Tuck tissue flames up through the logs — red outside, yellow inside.
Set the battery light in the middle, dim the room lights, and gather around.
Story rounds: each kid adds one sentence to the campfire tale. The flames 'grow' (add tissue) when the story gets exciting.

variations.easier: The teacher builds the fire; kids add flames and tell the story.
variations.harder: Shadow round: one flashlight behind the fire throws giant story shadows on the wall — act out the tale.

safety: Battery lights only — no real flames, ever, indoors. Keep the circle wide enough that no one trips into the 'fire'.

name: Shadow Puppet Matinee
tagline: Cardboard puppets, one flashlight, a dark room — the hottest-hour show.

materials.item: a white sheet or blank wall

setup: Hang the sheet or clear a blank wall. Test the flashlight distance — about 6 feet back gives big, sharp shadows. Pre-cut puppet blanks for little ones.
steps: Draw a character on black cardstock — animals read best in shadow — and cut it out.
Tape it to a stick. That's your actor.
Rehearse behind the sheet: figure out which way is up in shadow-land (it's backwards the first time, every time).
Groups of 3 get 5 minutes to stage a one-minute scene.
Matinee: lights down, audience seated, each troupe performs. Applause is mandatory.
Encore: the whole cast does a shadow dance finale behind the sheet.

variations.easier: Pre-cut animal shapes; kids tape and perform only.
variations.harder: Multi-light show: two flashlights at angles make double shadows — choreograph them.

safety: Scissors safety as always. Flashlights never pointed at eyes — the beam aims at the sheet, period.

name: Camp Week Kickoff
tagline: The opening assembly that turns 30 strangers into one camp: cheer, map, first mission.

materials.item: a big paper week-map or whiteboard
a camp cheer (made up on the spot)

setup: Draw the week-map: five big boxes labeled with each day's theme. Set chairs in a wide circle. Have name tags ready.
steps: Everyone writes a name tag with their name plus one summer thing they love.
Name game lightning round: each kid says their name with a move; the whole circle repeats it.
Invent the camp cheer together — three words, one stomp, one clap. Practice it twice.
Unveil the week-map: walk through each day's headline so the week has a shape.
First mission: mixed teams get one 15-minute challenge (chalk the camp motto on the walkway) and report back.
Close with the cheer. Camp has officially started.

variations.easier: Shorter circle, teacher-led cheer, and the mission is a group drawing instead of a challenge.
variations.harder: Legacy round: each week adds one box to a season-long map — by August the wall tells the whole summer.

safety: Keep the circle in shade if outdoors — opening assemblies run long and kids wilt. Water within reach.

name: Talent Showcase Night
tagline: A low-pressure camp talent night format: every act gets 90 seconds and a roaring crowd.
setup: Tape the sign-up sheet up at lunch — acts sign themselves up, no auditions. Mark the stage area and set out seating.
steps: Acts sign up in pairs or solos — every act gets exactly 90 seconds, timed kindly.
Emcees (two volunteers) introduce each act with a made-up fancy title.
The audience rule, stated up front: every act gets cheers, no act gets booed — that's the whole contract.
Between acts, the emcees run 30-second crowd games (stand up if you love pizza).
Finale: the counselors do a deliberately terrible act. The kids judge them, loudly.
Programs get signed like yearbooks afterward.

variations.easier: Group acts only, 60 seconds, and the teacher emcees.
variations.harder: Theme night: every act must involve water, or shadows, or things found outside — watch creativity spike.

safety: No live flames, no throwing acts, no rooftop anything — the emcees check each act's plan at sign-up. Keep volume neighbor-friendly after dark.

name: Star-Spangled Shoebox Parade
tagline: Decorate shoebox floats in red, white, and blue — then parade the whole route.

materials.item: red, white, and blue paper, streamers, and stickers

setup: Collect shoeboxes ahead — one per kid. Cut streamer lengths and sort the red/white/blue supplies into trays by color.
steps: Flip each shoebox upside down: that's the float base.
Cover it in paper — stripes, stars, or solid colors with sticker constellations.
Add streamers to the back so it flies while parading. Tie on a pull string.
Line up by height, count down from ten, and parade the route: around the building, past the office, back to the room.
Judging categories: most stars, best streamers, loudest cheers from the audience.
Floats go home the same day — parade glory is perishable.

variations.easier: Pre-covered boxes; kids add stickers and streamers only.
variations.harder: Night parade: tape glow bracelets to the floats and parade at dusk.

safety: Scissors supervision. Parade route checked ahead for tripping hazards and traffic — sidewalks and fields only, never streets.

name: Liberty Quiz Bowl
tagline: Team trivia on July 4th basics — the Declaration, the 13 colonies, the 50 stars.
setup: Write 20 to 30 questions on cards, easy to hard. Split the room into 3 or 4 teams. Set the scoreboard where everyone sees it.
steps: Sample rounds, all real facts: What year was the Declaration of Independence signed? (1776.) How many colonies became the first states? (13.) How many stars on the flag? (50 — one per state.) What city was the first capital under the Constitution? (New York.)
Teams huddle 15 seconds, then the captain answers.
Steal rule: a wrong answer bounces to the next team for half points.
Halftime show: each team performs its answer to 'what does freedom mean at camp?' in 30 seconds.
Winners get the Golden Bell until next year; everyone gets a sticker.
Fact-check any disputed answer together — the atlas and the encyclopedia outrank the loudest team.

variations.easier: True-or-false only, teams answer together with thumbs up or down.
variations.harder: Kids write the next year's question cards — the question-writers learn twice as much.

safety: Keep rivalry friendly: the emcee calls a reset the moment anyone's feelings get louder than the game.

name: Longest Day Shadow Track
tagline: Track one shadow from morning to afternoon on the solstice — the sun draws the graph.
setup: Plant the stick upright in a sunny paved spot first thing in the morning. Draw the first shadow outline in chalk and label it with the time.
steps: Every hour, on the hour, trace the shadow's new position in a new chalk color and log the time and length.
Predict at lunch: where will the 2 p.m. shadow fall? Mark guesses with initials.
At day's end, connect the dots: the shadow drew an arc across the pavement.
Read the arc together: shortest shadow = the sun at its highest = solar noon, near the longest day of the year.
Photo the finished arc for the camp board — the sun signed its work.

variations.easier: Three tracings only (morning, noon, afternoon) with the teacher handling the chalk.
variations.harder: Week-long edition: trace the noon shadow every day for a week and watch the arc creep.

safety: Never look directly at the sun while tracking — watch the shadow, not the source. Shade, hats, and water for the trackers; rotate the job so nobody bakes.

name: Giant Bubble Chase
tagline: Blow the biggest bubbles you can — then chase and pop them before they land.

materials.item: bubble solution (dish soap + water + a spoon of sugar)

setup: Mix the solution ahead: roughly 6 cups water, 1 cup dish soap, 1 tablespoon sugar — stir gently, no foam. Pour into shallow trays, one per 4 kids.
steps: Demo the slow pull: dip the big loop, lift it dripping, and walk backward — the bubble grows behind you.
Chasers line up downwind. Blowers launch; chasers pop before landing.
Rules of the chase: pop with a fingertip, not a face; one pop per bubble (no hogging).
Switch roles every 5 minutes — everyone blows, everyone chases.
Grand finale: the whole group launches at once and the field fills with bubbles.

variations.easier: Small wands, seated blowing, and the teacher does the chasing demo.
variations.harder: Bubble snake pit: everyone blows at once into one corner and counts how many bubbles fit in a hula hoop.

safety: Bubble solution stings eyes — keep a water bottle handy for rinses and remind kids to pop with fingers, not faces. Slippery when spilled: trays on grass, not pavement.

name: Ghost Garland String
tagline: Tissue ghosts, strung on yarn — the fastest room transformation in the Vault.
setup: Cut tissue into 8-inch squares — one per ghost. Cut yarn into 4-foot lengths and tie a loop at one end for hanging.
steps: Wrap a tissue square over a cotton ball and pinch it under the 'head'.
Tie a short piece of yarn snugly under the head to make the neck.
Draw two eyes and a surprised mouth with marker — every ghost gets a personality.
Tie each ghost to the long yarn, spacing them a hand-width apart.
Hang the garlands across the room and stand back: instant haunted hallway.

variations.easier: Use paper napkins instead of tissue and skip the cotton balls — flat ghosts tape straight to the yarn.
variations.harder: Add tiny paper hats or capes, and alternate ghosts with orange paper pumpkins on the string.

safety: Scissors stay at the table; little kids get pre-cut squares. Keep garlands above head height in walkways so nobody gets tangled.

name: Monster Masks
tagline: Cardstock monsters with 3D horns, fangs, and warts — built for the costume station.

materials.item: extras: paper scraps, cotton balls, foil

setup: Pre-cut a mask oval for the youngest kids; older kids trace and cut their own. Punch side holes for elastic, or tape a craft stick handle.
steps: Hold the oval to your face and mark where your eyes are — cut the eye holes wide.
Build the monster: glue on horns (folded paper triangles), fangs (white triangles along the mouth), warts (cotton balls or crumpled foil).
Color the whole face — green, purple, spotted, whatever your monster is.
Attach elastic through the side holes, or tape a craft stick as a handle.
Monster meet-and-greet: introduce your monster with a name and one silly power.

variations.easier: Use pre-cut masks and stick-on features only — no cutting at all.
variations.harder: Design a two-faced mask: hero on the outside, monster on the inside.

safety: Eye holes must stay big enough to see through clearly — no peeking through slits. Masks come off for running games.

name: Lollipop Ghost Treats
tagline: A tissue, a lollipop, a ribbon — the classic Halloween handout, made by the kids.
setup: Count lollipops — one per ghost, plus a few extras. Cut ribbon into 6-inch pieces.
steps: Drape a tissue over a lollipop so it hangs like a little ghost.
Pinch the tissue under the candy and tie it snugly with ribbon.
Draw two eyes and a tiny mouth on the front.
Line the ghosts up on the table — a whole haunted chorus.
Bag them up: instant Halloween handouts or party favors.

variations.easier: Skip the ribbon — a twist of the tissue under the candy holds fine for table display.
variations.harder: Write one kind note on the back of each ghost before bagging.

safety: Check the candy against the class allergy list first — offer stickers or pencils as the alternative for kids who can't have it. No unwrapping and eating during craft time; treats go home.

name: Pressed-Leaf Mandalas
tagline: Fall leaves arranged into perfect symmetrical circles — harvest math you can hang up.

materials.item: pressed or freshly fallen leaves in different colors

setup: Collect fallen leaves ahead — or send kids out with a bag first. Press them under books for a day if you want them flat.
steps: Sort your leaves by color and size — this is the planning step.
Find the center of your circle and place one special leaf there.
Build rings outward, repeating the same leaf in the same spots all the way around — symmetry is the game.
Glue each ring before starting the next so nothing slides.
Gallery walk: which mandala has the most rings? Which is the most symmetrical?

variations.easier: Use a paper plate with the ridges as ring guides, and only two leaf colors.
variations.harder: Photograph the mandala, then rebuild it from memory — or design one with 180-degree rotational symmetry only.

safety: Collect fallen leaves only — don't strip branches. Wash hands after handling outdoor leaves.

name: Costume Runway Walk
tagline: Every costume gets its strut: a runway, a narrator, and one big pose at the end.

materials.item: a long rug, tape line, or chalk path for the runway

setup: Lay the runway down the middle of the room. Line chairs along both sides for the audience. Pick your first narrator — or be it yourself.
steps: One kid at a time walks the runway in costume while the narrator announces them: 'And here comes… the bravest pirate in Room 4!'
At the end of the runway, strike one big pose and hold it for three seconds.
The audience gives a silent cheer — jazz hands only, so the next walker can hear their intro.
Walk back along the side and take a seat; the next walker goes.
Finale: everyone walks the runway together for the group photo.

variations.easier: Walk in pairs so shy kids have company.
variations.harder: Walkers invent a signature move and the audience votes on categories — silliest, spookiest, most creative.

safety: Costumes must let kids see and walk — nothing over the eyes on the runway, and long capes get held up or pinned. Clear the runway of bags and shoes first.

name: Costume Piece Relay
tagline: Each runner adds one costume piece before sprinting — by the anchor leg, everyone's a monster.

materials.item: a box of oversized costume pieces per team (hats, capes, glasses, gloves — thrift-store stuff)

setup: Split the costume box evenly between teams — same number of pieces each. Mark start and turn-around lines.
steps: Teams line up; the costume box sits at the start line.
On 'go,' the first runner puts on ONE piece, runs to the turn-around and back, and tags the next runner.
The next runner adds a second piece on top of the first — everyone keeps everything on.
Keep going until the last runner is wearing the whole team's collection.
Best-dressed team wins the style points; fastest team wins the race. Then swap boxes and go again.

variations.easier: Walk, don't run — and pieces go on over regular clothes, not instead of them.
variations.harder: Each runner must do their lap in character — the witch cackles, the robot clanks.

safety: Nothing that covers eyes or mouths while running, and no long trailing capes near feet. Pieces come off before anyone climbs or jumps.

name: Mystery Feel Boxes
tagline: Reach in and guess: peeled grapes, cold spaghetti — spooky-feeling, zero scares, lights on.

materials.item: shoeboxes with hand-holes cut in the lids

setup: Cut a hand-hole in each box lid and tape the lids on so nobody peeks. Fill each box with one mystery item and label it with a silly spooky name ('Witch's Eyeballs').
steps: Line the boxes up and read the spooky labels out loud — dramatic voice encouraged.
One at a time, reach in (no peeking!) and feel for ten seconds.
Whisper your guess to the teacher or write it on a slip — no shouting it out.
Rotate through every box, then reveal the real items one by one.
Vote: which one felt the spookiest? Which one fooled the most people?

variations.easier: Let kids look at the items first, then feel them blind — matching, not guessing.
variations.harder: Kids design their own feel-box items from the classroom and stump the next group.

safety: Check every food item against the class allergy list before it goes in a box. Hands get washed before and after — nothing from the boxes goes in mouths.

name: Monster Mash Dance Party
tagline: Freeze dance with monster moves called out — freeze in your spookiest pose.

materials.item: a speaker and a silly-spooky playlist (teacher's pick)

setup: Clear a dance floor. Make the playlist — spooky-but-silly songs, nothing actually scary for the little ones.
steps: Everyone dances. When the caller shouts a monster — 'ZOMBIE!' 'WITCH!' 'MUMMY!' — dance like it.
Music stops: freeze in your spookiest pose. Movers become the judges for one round.
Judges pick the three best freezes — those kids become callers for the next round.
New round, new caller, new monsters. Keep the poses coming.
Last song: everybody's-monster freestyle, then a group freeze for the photo.

variations.easier: No judging — everyone just freezes and unfreezes together.
variations.harder: Callers string two monsters together ('zombie-witch!') and dancers have to blend them.

safety: Dance floor stays clear of bags, chairs, and costume pieces that trip. Keep the volume at conversation-over-it level.

name: Apples on a String
tagline: Bite the hanging apple with no hands — all the bobbing fun, none of the shared water.

materials.item: a horizontal pole, branch, or clothesline to hang them from

setup: Tie a string around each apple stem — or through a cored hole — and hang them at chin height from the line. Space them an arm's length apart.
steps: Each kid stands in front of their own apple, hands behind their back.
On 'go,' bite the apple — no hands, no holding the string.
First bite counts as a point; most bites in two minutes wins the round.
Eat your apple when the round ends — you earned it.
Championship: the winners face off with the strings raised one notch higher.

variations.easier: Let kids steady the apple with one finger on the string.
variations.harder: Gently swing the apples before starting — moving targets.

safety: One apple per kid — no sharing bites. Check apple allergies first (rare, but ask). Watch for kids biting off more than they can chew; cut apples into wedges for anyone who struggles.

name: Pumpkin Volcano
tagline: A jack-o'-lantern that erupts: baking soda, vinegar, and dish soap, straight out of the grin.
setup: An adult cuts the top off the pumpkin and scoops it clean — kids do NOT do the knife work. Set the pumpkin on a tray (this gets messy). Pre-measure the baking soda into cups.
steps: Carve or draw the jack-o'-lantern face — keep the mouth wide for the eruption.
Spoon 3 tablespoons of baking soda into the pumpkin's hollow.
Add a squirt of dish soap and a few drops of orange food coloring.
Pour in half a cup of vinegar and step back — the volcano erupts out of the grin.
Ask the science question: what made it foam? (The acid and the base react and release gas.) Repeat with more vinegar.

variations.easier: Skip the carving — draw the face with marker and use an uncut pumpkin with the top off.
variations.harder: Test variables: does warm vinegar erupt more than cold? Does more soap make taller foam? Run it like an experiment.

safety: Adults do ALL knife work — scooping and carving are grown-up jobs, full stop. Vinegar stings eyes, so pour slowly and keep faces back from the eruption.

name: Candy Chromatography
tagline: Candy dyes split into rainbow rings on a coffee filter — real separation science, Halloween edition.
setup: Sort candies by color — one color per filter. Cut coffee filters into strips and draw a pencil dot (not pen!) near the bottom of each.
steps: Place one candy on the pencil dot and add a single drop of water on top of it.
Watch: the color bleeds out and creeps up the filter in a ring.
Wait two minutes, then lift the candy off — look at the rings left behind.
Compare colors: which candy's dye split into two colors? Which stayed one?
The reveal: one 'single' color is often a mix of dyes — the filter pulled them apart.

variations.easier: Use brown and green candies only — they show the clearest splits.
variations.harder: Predict first, then test: write down which candies you think hide two dyes, and check your predictions.

safety: Check the candy against the class allergy list. This is a look-don't-lick experiment — no tasting during the science.

name: Monster Slime Lab
tagline: Classic slime, monster-fied: googly eyes, glitter 'fur,' and stretch tests.
setup: Cover tables — slime finds everything. Pre-measure: half a cup of glue and half a cup of water per batch, mixed in each bowl.
steps: Stir half a teaspoon of baking soda into the glue-water mix.
Add food coloring and glitter — this is the monster's skin and fur.
Add one tablespoon of saline solution and stir; add a second if it's still sticky.
Knead it with your hands for two minutes — the stickiness works itself out.
Press in the googly eyes: your monster is alive. Stretch-test: how far before it snaps?

variations.easier: The teacher mixes the base; kids only do the coloring, glitter, and eyes.
variations.harder: Run the stretch test like an experiment: does more saline make it stretchier or snappier? Chart three batches.

safety: Slime is for hands, not mouths — no tasting, and wash hands when you're done. Skip this one for kids who still mouth everything, and check for skin sensitivities to glue or saline.

name: Haunted House Blueprints
tagline: Design a not-scary haunted house on paper: silly scares, secret passages, and a marked exit.
setup: Hand out graph paper and rulers — one set per designer or pair. Set the design rule up front: silly-spooky only, nothing that would scare a kindergartner.
steps: Draw the floor plan: entrance, three scare rooms, and a clearly marked EXIT.
Design one silly scare per room — a tickle tunnel, a room where the 'ghosts' compliment you, a floor that squeaks on purpose.
Add one secret passage and label how it works.
Trade blueprints with a neighbor: can they find the exit? Would a little kid laugh or cry at your scares?
Revise once based on the feedback, then post the blueprints as the Haunted Hallway gallery.

variations.easier: Design just one room instead of three, with a big EXIT arrow.
variations.harder: Add a materials list and a budget: what would your haunted house actually cost to build?

name: Apple Tasting Party
tagline: Taste-test apple varieties blind, vote for the class favorite, and graph the results.

materials.item: a knife and cutting board (adult only)

setup: An adult slices the apples into tasting wedges — kids don't do the cutting. Label the varieties A, B, C so the tasting is blind.
steps: Taste variety A: crunchy or soft? Sweet or tart? Everyone gives a thumbs up, sideways, or down.
Repeat for B, C, and D — cleanse the palate with a sip of water between.
Vote: one sticker per kid on the chart for your favorite.
Reveal the names — did the class favorite surprise anyone?
Graph it: bar chart of the votes, and one sentence about what the winning apple tasted like.

variations.easier: Two varieties only, and vote with a show of hands.
variations.harder: Add descriptive words to the chart — have tasters invent the vocabulary (snappy, honeyed, zippy).

safety: Adults do all the cutting. Check for apple and fruit allergies before tasting day, and keep the slices separate from other snacks.

name: Harvest Gratitude Circle
tagline: One thankful thought each, added to a paper harvest wreath — the season's quiet anchor.

materials.item: a large paper wreath cutout or paper-plate ring

setup: Cut a big wreath ring from butcher paper, or tape paper-plate rings together. Cut paper leaves — one per kid plus extras.
steps: Sit in a circle. Each person names one thing from this season they're thankful for — a person, a food, a moment.
Write it on a paper leaf (or dictate it for young writers).
One by one, tape your leaf to the wreath and say the word out loud.
When the wreath is full, hang it where the whole program can see it.
Closing: one thing you're looking forward to before winter.

variations.easier: Draw the thankful thing instead of writing it.
variations.harder: Write the why, not just the what — one sentence about why it matters.

name: Pumpkin Guts Sensory Bin
tagline: Scoop, squish, and sort: pumpkin pulp and seeds in the bin, tweezers for the scientists.

materials.item: a scooped pumpkin's pulp and seeds

setup: An adult scoops the pumpkin ahead of time — kids get the pulp, not the knife. Spread a sheet under the bin; this is gloriously messy.
steps: Tip the whole pumpkin's insides into the bin — pulp, seeds, strings, all of it.
Free explore: squish it, smell it, describe it. Slimy? Stringy? Cold?
The sort challenge: tweezers only — seeds in one cup, pulp in another.
Count the seeds in teams of ten. Which team harvested the most?
Save the seeds for roasting or planting; compost the pulp.

variations.easier: Hands only, no tweezers — just explore and describe.
variations.harder: Weigh the seed cups: does the biggest pile always weigh the most?

safety: Pumpkin seeds are a choking hazard for the littlest kids — close supervision, and seeds stay in the bin, not in mouths. Wash hands before and after.

name: Trunk-or-Treat Planning
tagline: Kids design the parking-lot Halloween: trunk themes, a traffic map, and the allergy-safe table.

materials.item: big paper for the parking-lot map

setup: Sketch the real parking lot outline on the big paper — or walk it first and pace it off. Make the volunteer sign-up sheet.
steps: Map it: draw every parking space on the lot map and number the trunks.
Theme brainstorm: each team pitches a trunk theme — under-the-sea, mad scientist, book characters — and claims a space.
Plan the traffic flow: one-way walking lanes, an entrance and an exit, so nobody bottlenecks.
Assign jobs: greeters, the allergy-safe treat table crew, the cleanup crew.
Send the sign-up sheet home: which family brings which trunk, and who staffs the allergy-safe table.

variations.easier: The teacher maps the lot; kids only pitch themes and vote.
variations.harder: Kids write the family letter themselves — date, time, what to bring, where to park.

safety: Cars stay parked with engines off for the whole event, and adults monitor the lot entrance. Plan the route so kids never walk behind reversing cars.

name: Reverse Trick-or-Treat
tagline: Flip the script: kids pack treat bags and deliver them to seniors and neighbors.
setup: Line up the delivery route ahead — a nearby senior center, or neighbors who've said yes. Buy sealed treats; check the allergy-safe options.
steps: Decorate the bags — Halloween on the outside, kindness on the inside.
Pack each bag: two or three sealed treats and one handmade thank-you card.
Walk the route in small groups, each with an adult.
Knock, smile, hand over the bag: 'Happy Halloween — this one's for you!'
Back at home base: share one reaction each. Who lit up the most?

variations.easier: Deliver within the building — the front office, the custodians, the younger classrooms.
variations.harder: Kids plan the route and write the ask-note to the senior center themselves.

safety: Small groups, an adult with every group, daylight or well-lit routes only. Sealed, store-bought treats only — nothing homemade for giving away. Check the allergy-safe options before packing.

name: Teal Pumpkin Project
tagline: Paint a pumpkin teal and run the allergy-safe treat table — Halloween for every kid.

materials.item: teal paint or a teal pumpkin sign

setup: Paint the pumpkin teal ahead of time, or let the kids do it as the craft. Set up TWO treat containers: candy, and the teal non-food box.
steps: The meaning: a teal pumpkin on a porch means 'we have allergy-safe, non-food treats here.'
Paint your teal pumpkin — or make a teal pumpkin sign for the door.
Stock the teal box: stickers, pencils, glow bracelets, bouncy balls — nothing edible.
Practice the line: 'Would you like candy or a teal treat?' Every kid gets asked, every kid gets a choice.
Put the teal pumpkin where trick-or-treaters can see it, with the teal box right beside the candy.

variations.easier: Print a teal pumpkin sign instead of painting — same meaning, zero dry time.
variations.harder: Kids survey the neighborhood: how many teal pumpkins can they spot on Halloween night?

safety: Keep the non-food treats truly separate from the candy — different box, different scoop, no mix-ups. Check that small non-food items aren't choking hazards for the youngest visitors.

name: Trick-or-Treat Route Map
tagline: Map the safe route before the big night: lit streets, buddy pairs, and crossing points.

materials.item: printed neighborhood maps or big paper

setup: Print simple street maps of the neighborhood around the school or program — or draw the main streets on big paper together.
steps: Mark home base on the map — that's where the route starts and ends.
Trace the route: stick to well-lit streets and sidewalks, and mark every street crossing with an X.
Pair up: every kid gets a buddy, and buddies never separate — draw the pairs on the map's corner.
Mark the safe stops: houses of people you know, the teal pumpkin houses, the well-lit corners.
Walk the rules out loud: stay on sidewalks, cross at corners, one adult per group, home by the agreed time.

variations.easier: The teacher pre-marks the route; kids add the buddy pairs and safe-stop stickers.
variations.harder: Kids plan a second route for a different start point and compare which is safer.

safety: This is the safety activity: daylight planning for a nighttime event. The standing rules — reflective gear or glow sticks, an adult with every group, no entering homes — get said out loud and written on the map.

name: Thankful Turkey Handprints
tagline: A handprint turkey with a feather for every thankful thought.
setup: Trace a hand template on brown paper — one body per kid. Cut colored paper into feather strips, about 8 inches long.
steps: Trace your hand on brown paper and cut it out — the fingers are the turkey's tail feathers.
Cut a round body and a smaller head from brown paper; glue the head on top.
Add googly eyes or marker eyes, an orange triangle beak, and a red wattle.
Write one thankful thought on each paper feather, then glue the feathers in a fan behind the body.
Line the turkeys up on the wall — a whole flock of gratitude.

variations.easier: Use a pre-traced hand and write the thankful thoughts for the youngest kids.
variations.harder: Make the feathers 3D — fold each one down the middle — and write a whole paragraph of thanks on the back of the body.

safety: Scissors stay at the table; little kids get pre-cut bodies and feathers.
inclusion: Pre-cut pieces for little hands; dictate thankful thoughts for pre-writers.

name: Paper Cornucopia
tagline: A rolled-paper horn of plenty, stuffed with a paper harvest.

materials.item: large brown paper or grocery bags

setup: Cut brown paper into 18-inch squares. Set out colored paper for the fruit and vegetables.
steps: Roll a paper square into a cone — overlap the edges and tape the seam. This is the horn.
Curl the narrow end slightly to one side, the way a real cornucopia curves.
Draw, color, and cut out paper apples, pumpkins, grapes, and corn — big and bold.
Stuff the harvest into the wide end so it spills over the rim.
Set the cornucopias down the center of the table as the feast centerpiece.

variations.easier: Make mini horns from half-sheets and fill them with three paper fruits only.
variations.harder: Weave thin paper strips over the cone in a basket pattern before stuffing it.

safety: Scissors stay at the table. Big cones get a tape ring on the seam so they hold their shape.
inclusion: Pre-rolled cones available; partner rolling for limited grip strength.

name: Friendsgiving Place Cards
tagline: Hand-drawn place cards with one reason each guest is loved.
setup: Fold cards in half so they stand like tents. Write every guest's name on a slip of paper for the draw.
steps: Draw a name from the pile — that's the guest you're honoring.
Write their name big on the front of the tent card.
Inside, finish the sentence: 'I'm glad you're at this table because...'
Decorate the card with their favorite things — ask around if you're not sure.
Set the cards at the friendsgiving table before anyone sits down.

variations.easier: Write the name and one word ('funny', 'kind') instead of a sentence.
variations.harder: Add a tiny portrait of your guest on the back of the card.

inclusion: Draw instead of write; name cards can be dictated.

name: Harvest Weave Placemats
tagline: Paper-strip weaving in harvest colors — the table sets itself.
setup: Cut one sheet per kid into a 9x12 frame (leave the middle open) for the warp, and cut 1-inch strips in harvest colors for the weft.
steps: Lay the frame flat — these are your straight-up-and-down strips.
Weave a colored strip over, under, over, under across the frame.
Push each strip snug against the last and keep going to the bottom.
Glue the strip ends to the frame edges so nothing slides loose.
Optional: cover both sides with clear contact paper so the placemat survives the feast.

variations.easier: Use wide 2-inch strips — fewer weaves, same harvest look.
variations.harder: Weave a pattern: two orange, one brown, repeating — or spell initials with strip colors.

safety: Scissors stay at the table; pre-cut strips for the youngest weavers.
inclusion: Wide strips for easier weaving; pre-cut strips for the youngest.

name: Turkey Tag
tagline: The farmers are coming — gobble, dodge, and don't get caught.

materials.item: pool noodles or flag belts (one per farmer)

setup: Set boundaries with cones. Pick 2 farmers to start; everyone else is a turkey. Farmers hold pool noodles; turkeys tuck nothing — just run.
steps: Turkeys scatter inside the boundaries when you shout 'Gobble!'
Farmers chase and tag turkeys with a gentle noodle tap.
Tagged turkeys freeze and flap their wings until a free turkey high-fives them back in.
After three minutes, switch farmers so everyone gets to chase.
Last round: one farmer, and the turkeys who survive get to pick the next game.

variations.easier: Play with walking only and shrink the boundaries for little legs.
variations.harder: Add a safe 'barn' zone — turkeys inside are safe but can only stay five seconds.

safety: Noodle taps stay gentle and below the shoulders. Clear the field of holes and sticks first.
inclusion: Walking-only rounds; a seated 'barn guard' role keeps everyone in the game.
why_it_works: Played in short 3-minute rounds, it works as a structured movement break — research finds active breaks under 10 minutes improve on-task behavior (Deakin University, IJRESS Jan 2026).

name: Pumpkin Bucket Toss
tagline: Toss mini pumpkins into harvest buckets from the line.

materials.item: mini pumpkins or orange beanbags (6 per team)
chalk or tape for the throw line

setup: Set buckets 6 feet from the throw line for little kids, 10 for older ones. Split pumpkins evenly between teams.
steps: Teams line up behind the throw line, pumpkins in hand.
One at a time, toss a pumpkin toward your team's bucket.
Count only the pumpkins that land IN the bucket — rim bounces don't count.
Move the line back two feet every round the whole team scores.
Winning team picks the harvest song for cleanup.

variations.easier: Use big laundry baskets close up, and let little kids step over the line.
variations.harder: Score it: far bucket 3 points, middle 2, near 1 — teams aim for the big total.

safety: Real mini pumpkins only — nothing heavy enough to hurt. Toss toward the buckets, never at people.
inclusion: Move the line closer; bigger buckets for easier success.

name: Harvest Basket Relay
tagline: Teams fill their harvest basket one armload at a time.

materials.item: one basket or box per team

setup: Pile the 'crops' at the far cone. Give each team a basket at the start line.
steps: First runner sprints to the pile and grabs ONE crop.
Carry it back — no throwing the crop to a teammate.
Drop it in the team basket and tag the next runner.
Keep going until the pile is empty, then count the baskets.
Fullest basket wins — then everybody helps carry the harvest inside.

variations.easier: Walk instead of run, and let kids carry two crops at a time.
variations.harder: Each runner must name something they're thankful for before they can grab a crop.

safety: Keep the running lanes separated so nobody collides at the pile.
inclusion: Walk instead of run; carry two crops to shorten the distance.

name: Cranberry Structures
tagline: Toothpicks and cranberries: who builds the tallest harvest tower?
setup: Rinse the cranberries and pat dry — wet ones slide off the toothpicks. Hand out 30 cranberries and a pile of toothpicks per kid.
steps: Sketch your tower first: triangles hold weight, squares wobble.
Push a toothpick into a cranberry — that's your first joint.
Build a triangle base, then stack triangles upward.
Test as you go: does it stand on its own? Wobble means rebuild the base wider.
Measure the finished towers — tallest freestanding tower wins the harvest crown.

variations.easier: Build flat shapes on the table — stars, snowflakes, letters — instead of towers.
variations.harder: Add a weight test: how many pennies can the top hold before it tips?

safety: Toothpicks are pointy — build on the table, never sword-fight. Check the class allergy list before using real cranberries; pom-poms build exactly the same.
inclusion: Build flat shapes instead of towers; partner roles for every step.

name: Turkey Baster Relay
tagline: Move the 'cranberries' with nothing but a turkey baster and air.

materials.item: cones for start and finish lines

setup: Set a bowl of pom-poms at the start line and an empty bucket at the finish line, about 10 feet apart, per team.
steps: Squeeze the baster bulb, press the tip against a pom-pom, and let go — suction grabs it.
Carry the pom-pom to the finish bucket without touching it with your hands.
Drop it in, run the baster back, and hand it to the next runner.
Dropped it? Pick it up with the baster only — fingers don't count.
First team to move all their cranberries wins. Then talk: what made the grip work — air pressure pushing back in.

variations.easier: Use big pom-poms and a short carry distance; let little kids use two hands on the baster.
variations.harder: Blow-only round: no suction allowed — push the pom-pom across the table with baster air.

safety: Basters point at pom-poms, never at faces. Allergy-safe by design: the 'cranberries' are pom-poms, so there are no food allergies to check. Wash basters before and after if they were ever near real food.
inclusion: Big pom-poms, short distance; two hands on the baster.

name: Shake-a-Jar Butter
tagline: Cream, a jar, and ten minutes of shaking: that's butter.

materials.item: small jars with tight lids (one per pair)

setup: Pour cream into each jar — fill only halfway. Screw the lids on tight. Check the class allergy list before you start.
steps: Shake the jar hard — the cream sloshes, then thickens into whipped cream. Keep going.
Keep shaking past the whipped stage: suddenly a yellow lump separates from thin liquid. That's butter and buttermilk.
Pour off the liquid, add a pinch of salt, and give it five more shakes.
Spread it on a cracker and taste the science — you made that.
Talk it through: shaking smashed the fat droplets together until they stuck.

variations.easier: One big jar for the whole group — everyone takes a 30-second shake turn.
variations.harder: Run a race: salted jar vs. unsalted — does one turn to butter first?

safety: Dairy check first: kids with dairy allergies take the official timer role and observe the science — no tasting without an adult's say-so. Jars stay closed while shaking.
inclusion: One big group jar with 30-second shake turns; timer role for dairy-free kids.
why_it_works: Hands-on making beats screen time: the APA's Sept 2026 report finds learning sticks when kids apply knowledge off-screen — and nothing is more off-screen than shaking cream into butter.

name: Friendsgiving Potluck Plan
tagline: The class plans its own friendsgiving feast — sign-up sheet and all.
setup: Draw the feast table on the big paper: drinks, mains, sides, desserts. Some families say 'harvest feast' instead of 'friendsgiving' — both names are welcome here.
steps: Brainstorm the menu together — every kid names one dish they'd love to see.
Sort the dishes into drinks, mains, sides, and desserts on the table map.
Families sign up for ONE dish each — nobody cooks the whole feast.
Every signed-up dish gets an ingredient card: list everything in it.
Assign jobs for the day: greeters, table setters, drink pourers, cleanup crew.

variations.easier: Teacher picks a simple fixed menu (three dishes) and kids only do the sign-up and jobs.
variations.harder: Kids cost out the feast: price each dish and build the shopping list on a budget.

safety: Check the class allergy list BEFORE the sign-up goes home — every dish needs its ingredient card, and keep one table nut-free.
inclusion: Fixed 3-dish menu option; jobs assigned by interest, not just volunteers.

name: Friendsgiving Story Circle
tagline: Pair up, trade a favorite memory, introduce your partner's story.
setup: No setup — just a circle of chairs and two minutes of quiet to think of a favorite memory with a friend.
steps: Pair up with someone you don't know well.
Each person tells their partner one favorite memory — two minutes each.
Come back to the circle. Now INTRODUCE your partner and retell THEIR story.
The partner gives a thumbs-up if the retelling got it right.
Close: one word each about what makes a good friend.

variations.easier: Skip the retelling — partners just share one thing they're thankful the other person taught them.
variations.harder: Make it a story chain: each pair's memory has to connect to the last pair's somehow.

inclusion: Share one thankful word instead of a story; listening counts fully.

name: Gratitude Alphabet Circle
tagline: A to Z around the circle: one thankful word per letter.
setup: No setup — circle up and pick who starts with A.
steps: First kid says something they're thankful for that starts with A — 'apples', 'Aunt May'.
Next kid takes B, then C, all the way around.
Stuck on a letter? The group gets ten seconds to shout suggestions.
Letters like Q, X, and Z allow 'thankful for' plus any word — no shame in 'xylophones'.
Finish at Z with a group cheer for the alphabet of thanks.

variations.easier: Do it in teams — each team takes every other letter.
variations.harder: Hard mode: no repeats from last week's circle, and X must be a real word.

inclusion: Team play for shy kids; passing allowed on any letter.

name: Thankful Jar Shares
tagline: Slips of gratitude in a jar, drawn and read aloud.
setup: Set the jar where everyone can reach it all week — it fills up before the share day.
steps: All week, kids drop in slips: 'I'm thankful for...' — names optional.
On share day, circle up and shake the jar.
Draw slips one at a time and read each aloud.
After each one, the group guesses who wrote it — or the writer claims it.
Save the week's slips in an envelope: the year's gratitude archive.

variations.easier: Do it in one sitting — five minutes of writing, then read them all.
variations.harder: Sort the slips into categories (people, places, things, moments) and graph which wins.

inclusion: Draw or dictate slips; anonymous by default.

name: Gratitude All Year
tagline: A gratitude practice for everyone — no holiday required.
setup: Give every kid a small booklet — this is their all-year gratitude log. Say it plainly: not every family celebrates Thanksgiving, and gratitude doesn't need a holiday.
steps: Decorate the cover: 'My Gratitude Log' and your name.
Write or draw three good things from TODAY — tiny counts: warm socks, a joke, lunch.
Share one with a partner if you want to — sharing is optional, always.
Set the rhythm: one page a week, every week, all year.
Check back monthly: flip through and notice how the good things stack up.

variations.easier: Draw instead of write — three pictures of good things per page.
variations.harder: Add a monthly 'gratitude letter': write one real thank-you note to someone outside the program.

inclusion: Draw instead of write; sharing always optional.

name: Food Drive Planning
tagline: Kids plan the whole canned-food drive: goal, posters, collection crew.
setup: Call the local food bank or pantry first (teacher job) to confirm what they accept and when to deliver.
steps: Set the goal together: 100 cans? One can per kid per week?
Make posters: what to bring, where the bins are, the deadline.
Build the collection bins from boxes — decorate them loud.
Assign the crew: bin monitors, counters, delivery team.
Count day: tally everything, celebrate the total, deliver together.

variations.easier: Run a one-day mini drive: goal of one bag per kid, counted the same afternoon.
variations.harder: Kids write the thank-you notes to every family that donated.

safety: Cans only — no open or homemade food in the bins. Heavy boxes get carried by adults.
inclusion: Poster, counter, and greeter roles for every mobility level.

name: Thank-You Cards for School Staff
tagline: Cards for the custodians, cafeteria crew, and bus drivers — the holiday heroes.
setup: List the staff the kids actually see: custodians, cafeteria crew, bus drivers, office staff, crossing guards.
steps: Each kid picks one staff member — no doubles until everyone is covered.
Write what that person DOES that helps you: 'You keep our halls clean.'
Add a drawing of them doing that job — capes optional.
Sign every card from the whole class.
Deliver them in person as a group — the delivery is the best part.

variations.easier: Make one giant class card per staff member instead of individual ones.
variations.harder: Kids interview their staff member first: 'What's the hardest part of your day?' — then write the card.

inclusion: One giant class card option; dictate the message.

name: Blessings Bags
tagline: Pack snack-and-supply bags for neighbors who need them.

materials.item: sealed store-bought snacks (granola bars, fruit cups)
socks, hand warmers, or travel toiletries

setup: Confirm the drop-off spot first (teacher job): a shelter, pantry, or community fridge. Buy sealed snacks only.
steps: Decorate each bag with markers — bright and kind.
Assembly line: one snack, one drink box, one pair of socks, one toiletry per bag.
Tuck in a handwritten note: 'Someone in your neighborhood packed this for you.'
Count and stack the finished bags.
Deliver together to the drop-off spot the same week.

variations.easier: Pack two bags as a whole group — one bag, everybody adds one item.
variations.harder: Kids plan the next round: what would YOU want in a bag on a cold night?

safety: Sealed store-bought snacks only — nothing homemade or opened. Check snack labels against the class allergy list if any bags stay in the room.
inclusion: Seated assembly line; decorating counts as full participation.

name: Turkey Code Feathers
tagline: Invent a symbol code, encode a turkey fact on feathers, trade and decode.
setup: Cut a simple turkey body and 8 feather shapes per kid. Feathers get taped on after the coding is done.
steps: Invent your symbols: draw one symbol for each letter A–Z (younger kids do A–M). This is your code key — keep it secret.
Pick a true turkey fact and encode it, one letter per feather.
Tape the coded feathers onto your turkey body.
Trade turkeys with a partner and decode theirs using THEIR key.
Share the most surprising fact the group decoded.

variations.easier: Use a ready-made symbol bank and encode just 3 letters.
variations.harder: Encode a whole riddle across two turkeys and let another pair crack it.

safety: Scissors stay at the table; pre-cut bodies and feathers for little kids.
inclusion: Symbol bank for a head start; drawing-only codes welcome; encode in a home language with a translated key.

name: Cornucopia Catch
tagline: Build paper cornucopias, then invent your own catch game — rules and all.
setup: Set out paper and tape per team of 3–4. Cut a pile of paper produce up front so building starts fast.
steps: Build 3 paper cornucopias sturdy enough to hold, catch, and toss.
Test: toss paper produce between teammates and catch it in the horn.
Now invent your own game: teams write the rules, the scoring, and a name.
Rotate: play another team's game exactly by their rules.
Vote: funniest rules, trickiest catch, best team name.

variations.easier: Build one big team cornucopia and play catch in a circle.
variations.harder: Add a points zone on the floor — long catches into the horn score double.

safety: Scissors stay at the table. Toss paper produce only, never at faces.
why_it_works: Student-designed endings — inventing the game's rules — are the 2026 STEM flourish research flags as most engaging: kids own the challenge instead of just following it.
inclusion: Pre-rolled cone templates; seated tossing; rules can be dictated and scribed.

name: Thanksgiving Table Build
tagline: Toothpicks and glue: build a table with at most 4 legs that holds the feast.
setup: Cover the table with wax paper — glue peels right off. Hand out toothpicks and glue per team.
steps: The constraint: a table with AT MOST 4 legs, standing on its own.
Sketch the leg design first — triangles beat squares for strength.
Build on the wax paper; let the glue set (build one day, test the next if you can).
Load books one at a time onto the tabletop; record the max before it fails.
Compare: which leg designs held the most? What would you change?

variations.easier: Build with thicker skewers and test with paperback books only.
variations.harder: Limit it to 20 toothpicks total — the constraint forces smarter design.

safety: Toothpicks are pointy — build on the table, never sword-fight. Check glue bottles for clogs before frustrated squeezing starts.
inclusion: Thicker skewers for easier grip; team roles (planner, builder, tester); test narrated aloud so everyone follows the results.

name: Elf Zipline Delivery
safety: Keep the line below shoulder height; no loops of string around necks or fingers.
setup: Pre-cut string lengths and poke a hole near the rim of each cup for the paper-clip hook.
steps: Tie the string tight between two points, one end higher than the other.
Hook a paper cup to the line with a paper clip so it slides freely.
Load a pom-pom gift into the cup and release it from the high end.
Time the trip. Try a steeper line and a flatter line. Which delivers faster?
Challenge: deliver two gifts in one trip without losing either.
tagline: String a zipline across the room and race to deliver the gifts fastest.

variations.easier: Use a short line between two chairs and deliver one gift at a time.
variations.harder: Add a marked drop zone and score points for landing the gift inside it.

materials.item: small cardboard trays or box lids
books or a board for the ramp
cotton balls or small blocks (the gifts)

name: Sleigh and Slope Run
safety: Test sleds on the floor, not off tables; clear the landing zone of feet.
setup: Stack books at one end of a table to make a sturdy ramp; tape the top so it can't slide.
steps: Build a sled: tape straws under a cardboard tray as runners.
Load three cotton-ball gifts onto the sled.
Release the sled from the top of the ramp.
If gifts fall off, redesign: add sides, lower the load, or change the runners.
Final run: which team's sled carries all three gifts the farthest?
tagline: Build a mini sled that carries gifts down a ramp without spilling.

variations.easier: Run the sled empty first, then add gifts one at a time.
variations.harder: Steepen the ramp and time the runs; fastest clean run wins.

materials.item: small clear plastic jars with lids
glitter, foam beads, and paper-hole-punch dots (the snow)
a spoonful of clear glue (optional, slows the fall)
small waterproof figurines or bottle-brush trees

name: Snow Globe Slow-Fall Lab
safety: Plastic jars only for kids; adult tightens and tapes the lid shut.
setup: Set out jars and snow ingredients in separate cups; hot-glue trees to lids ahead of time if kids are under 7.
steps: Glue a tiny tree or figure to the inside of the jar lid and let it set.
Fill the jar nearly full with water and add a spoonful of clear glue.
Try one kind of snow at a time. Shake, then time how long the snow takes to settle.
Record each snow type's fall time on a chart.
Pick the slowest snow for the final globe, then seal the lid with tape.
tagline: Build a real snow globe, then hunt for the slowest-falling snow.

variations.easier: Skip the timing; just build the globe with the snow you like best.
variations.harder: Graph all the fall times and write one sentence about why the slowest one won.

materials.item: a toy animal or pom-pom (the reindeer)

name: Reindeer Shelter Storm Test
safety: Fan stays on low; fingers and loose string stay away from the blades.
setup: Mark a test line on the table two feet from the fan; sort building materials into bins.
steps: Build a shelter big enough to fit your reindeer inside.
Set the shelter on the test line and place the reindeer inside.
Turn the fan on low for ten seconds: the blizzard is here.
Did the roof lift? Did the walls fall? Rebuild the weak spots.
Test again on a higher fan speed for the brave.
tagline: Build a tiny barn that survives a ten-second blizzard from a fan.

variations.easier: Test with a hair dryer on cool from far away instead of a fan.
variations.harder: Add a rule: the shelter must have a door the reindeer can walk through.

materials.item: a small gift bag with blocks inside (the weighted stocking)

name: Stocking Holder Build
safety: Test on sturdy low tables only; stand clear in case the holder tips during testing.
setup: Fill each gift bag with the same number of blocks so every stocking weighs the same.
steps: Design a holder that clamps or hooks onto the table edge.
Hang the weighted stocking from your holder.
Let go slowly. If the table tips or the holder slides, redesign.
Test three times in a row. It counts if it holds all three.
Decorate the winning holders and vote on the cleverest clamp.
tagline: Engineer a hook that hangs a full stocking off a table edge without tipping.

variations.easier: Start with a clothespin clip design; improve it from there.
variations.harder: Add a weight rule: hold two stockings at once.

materials.item: two tables or chairs (workshop and sled stations)

name: Gift Conveyor Design
safety: Keep the conveyor off the floor where feet walk; tape joints so tubes can't roll away.
setup: Set the two stations about six feet apart; sort tubes and rails where teams can reach them.
steps: Plan a path for the presents: rails, tubes, or a string pull-belt.
Build your conveyor between the two stations.
Launch a present from the workshop. No hands after it starts moving.
If a present gets stuck, find the jam and rebuild that section.
Run a full delivery of five presents. Fastest jam-free line wins.
tagline: Move presents from the workshop to the sled with no hands after launch.

variations.easier: Shorten the run to three feet and use one straight tube.
variations.harder: Add a hill: the present must climb before it rolls down.

name: Cookie Dissolve Race
safety: Check for dairy, egg, wheat, and nut allergies first; use dairy-free milk and allergy-safe cookies where needed. Wash hands before tasting.
setup: Pour milk into cups ahead of time; keep cookie packages sealed until the activity starts.
steps: Look at the three cookies. Predict which will dissolve first and write it down.
Drop one cookie into each cup of milk at the same time.
Watch and wait. Note the order the cookies soften and fall apart.
Taste-test a fresh cookie of each kind after the race.
Compare results to predictions. Did the crunchiest cookie win or lose?
tagline: Drop three kinds of cookies in milk and time which one melts first.

variations.easier: Race just two cookie kinds and skip the chart.
variations.harder: Try warm milk vs cold milk and compare the times.

materials.item: instant snow powder (sold as faux snow)

name: Instant Snow Polymers
safety: Not edible: nobody tastes the powder or the snow. Adult pours the powder for kids under 8.
setup: Pre-measure powder into small cups; set out water pitchers and bowls.
steps: Look at the dry powder with a magnifying glass. Describe it.
Add water one spoonful at a time and stir.
Watch it puff up. Keep adding until it stops growing.
Scoop the snow with your hands. How does it feel compared to real snow?
Write one sentence about what you think the powder did with the water.
tagline: Turn a spoonful of powder into a bowl of fluffy snow and figure out why.

variations.easier: Make one big shared bowl and explore it together.
variations.harder: Test two water amounts and compare which snow is fluffier.

name: Dancing Cranberries
safety: Vinegar fizz can splash: keep faces back from the cup and wipe spills right away.
setup: Set out cups, a cranberry bowl, and measured spoons of baking soda.
steps: Fill a cup halfway with water and stir in a spoonful of baking soda.
Drop in five dried cranberries. Watch: they sink.
Slowly pour in a splash of vinegar.
Watch the cranberries rise, dance, and sink again as bubbles grab them.
Try more or fewer cranberries. How many can dance at once?
tagline: Make dried cranberries bounce and bob in a fizzy cup.

variations.easier: Do it as a group demo with one big cup everyone can see.
variations.harder: Count how many trips one cranberry makes in a minute.

materials.item: stickers (stars, trees) for the start and finish

name: Paper Maze Swap
safety: None beyond the usual pencil rules.
setup: Hand out graph paper; keep extra sheets nearby for maze redesigns.
steps: Draw a maze on graph paper with one clear start and one finish.
Hide a holiday prize inside: a star sticker at the finish.
Test-solve your own maze to prove it can be finished.
Swap mazes with a partner and solve theirs without lifting your pencil.
Rate it: too easy, just right, or impossible? Tell the designer.
tagline: Draw a holiday maze, swap it, and race to solve someone else's.

variations.easier: Draw on plain paper with wide paths and no dead ends.
variations.harder: Add a rule: the solver must collect three hidden stars before the finish.

name: Gift Wrap Measure-Up
safety: Scissors safety for younger kids; pre-cut starter pieces if needed.
setup: Wrap nothing in advance; keep boxes and paper at a measuring station.
steps: Pick a box. Guess how many paper squares it would take to cover it.
Wrap the box for real and count the paper you used.
Measure each side of the box with a ruler and write the numbers down.
Try a second box. This time measure first, then predict.
Was your second prediction closer? The measurer's edge is real.
tagline: Estimate the paper a box needs, then measure and see who was closest.

variations.easier: Wrap one box and just compare guess vs result.
variations.harder: Compute the box's surface area from your measurements and compare.

materials.item: reindeer tokens (paper clips or small toys)

name: Reindeer Grid Coding
safety: None beyond the usual paper-and-scissors rules.
setup: Print grids ahead; cut arrow-card sets into envelopes, one set per kid.
steps: Place your reindeer on the start square and a star on the barn square.
Lay out arrow cards to plan the whole route before moving anything.
Run the program: move the reindeer one square per card.
Bug! If you crash into a wall, go back and fix the cards.
Trade grids with a partner and run their route.
tagline: Program a reindeer across a grid with arrow cards: no screens needed.

variations.easier: Use a 3x3 grid with the barn two squares away.
variations.harder: Add blocked squares the route must go around.

materials.item: washable paint, thinned with a little water
big paper sheets or a tray

name: Ornament Pendulum Paint
safety: Wear smocks; cover the table. Paint stays off faces and mouths; wash hands after.
setup: Poke a small hole in the bottom of each cup; tie the bell inside and the string outside. Set up one station at a time to avoid collisions.
steps: Hang the cup from a chair back or a held stick so it swings freely.
Tape big paper under the cup.
Pour a little thinned paint into the cup and pull it to the side.
Let go and watch it drip-paint spirals as it swings.
Change the pull length or add a second color and compare the patterns.
tagline: Swing a jingle-bell pendulum and let it drip-paint a holiday swirl.

variations.easier: Swing one color over a small paper plate.
variations.harder: Time the swings and try to paint matching patterns twice.

materials.item: clear plastic bottles with tight lids

name: Blizzard in a Bottle
safety: Adult tightens the lid, then tapes it shut. Oily bottles stay on the table, not on laps.
setup: Pre-fill bottles two-thirds with water; keep oil and glitter in pourable cups.
steps: Add a splash of oil and a pinch of glitter to your bottle.
Add one drop of white paint for cloudy storm water.
Cap it tight. Adult tapes the lid.
Shake hard: blizzard! Then set it down and watch the snow settle.
Tip it slowly side to side and watch the glitter swirl like wind.
tagline: Shake up a winter storm in a bottle and watch the glitter settle like snow.

variations.easier: Use water and glitter only; skip the oil.
variations.harder: Time how long the storm takes to calm for three different glitter amounts.

name: Dreidel Spin Math
safety: Small tokens are a choking hazard for kids under 4; keep them off the floor.
setup: Print the four dreidel letters and their meanings on a chart: nun (nothing), gimel (all), hey (half), shin (put one in).
steps: Learn the four sides: nun takes nothing, gimel takes all, hey takes half, shin puts one in.
Each player spins 10 times and tallies every result.
Add up your tallies. Which letter came up most?
Compare with the table: did everyone get similar results?
Play a real round with tokens in the pot, using the letter rules.
tagline: Spin the dreidel, tally the letters, and find out which side wins.

variations.easier: Just spin and act out the letter: gimel means a big cheer.
variations.harder: Track 50 spins as a group and graph which letter won.

materials.item: a printed list of the seven principles (Nguzo Saba)

name: Kwanzaa Principle Cards
safety: None beyond the usual classroom rules.
setup: Write the seven principles with one-line meanings on the board: Umoja (unity), Kujichagulia (self-determination), Ujima (collective work), Ujamaa (cooperative economics), Nia (purpose), Kuumba (creativity), Imani (faith).
steps: Make two cards for each principle: one with the name, one with a kid action (for Umoja: 'include someone new at lunch').
Shuffle all 14 cards face down.
Flip two at a time. Keep the pair if the name matches its action.
Read each match out loud when you win it.
Finish by naming which principle your family or class already lives.
tagline: Match the seven principles to everyday kid actions in a memory game.

variations.easier: Play with the principle list visible on the board.
variations.harder: Invent your own eighth action card for a principle and defend the match.

materials.item: one wrapped gift (or a wrapped box of treats to share)

name: Story Gift Pass
safety: Pass gently; no grabbing. If treats are inside, check allergies before sharing.
setup: Wrap the gift; print or write a short story packed with the words left and right.
steps: Sit in a circle. One person holds the wrapped gift.
The reader reads the story slowly.
Every time you hear 'left', pass the gift left. 'Right' passes right.
Keep listening; the gift keeps moving.
Whoever holds it when the story ends unwraps it (or shares the treats).
tagline: Pass the gift left and right as the story says, and see who unwraps it.

variations.easier: Use a ball instead of a gift and skip the unwrapping.
variations.harder: Write your own left-right story as a group first.

materials.item: a bird feeder nearby helps a lot

name: Winter Bird Watch Tally
safety: Watch from inside or a safe spot; never approach or touch wild birds.
setup: Set up near a window with a view of a tree or feeder; print simple tally sheets.
steps: Sit quietly for ten minutes and watch.
Make a tally mark every time a bird lands.
Note the color and size of each visitor: big brown, tiny gray, red chest.
Compare sheets: did everyone see the same birds?
Repeat on another day and see if the numbers change.
tagline: Spend ten quiet minutes counting the birds that visit in winter.

variations.easier: Just count total birds; skip colors and sizes.
variations.harder: Graph a week of counts and spot the busiest visiting time.

materials.item: cotton balls or tissue for smudging
white paint pens or chalk for stars

name: Northern Lights Pastels
safety: Oil pastels stain: wear smocks and wash hands after. Keep pastels away from mouths.
setup: Cover tables with paper; set out pastel sets and smudging cotton.
steps: Draw wavy ribbons of green and purple across the black paper.
Smudge the colors upward with a cotton ball to make them glow.
Add a dark mountain silhouette along the bottom.
Dot tiny white stars above the lights.
Hang the finished skies together as a winter gallery.
tagline: Smudge oil pastels into glowing auroras on black paper.

variations.easier: Use one color ribbon plus stars.
variations.harder: Layer three colors and blend them into a smooth gradient.

name: Snow Paint Spray
safety: Food coloring stains clothes and gloves; dress for mess and cold. Spray at snow, never at faces.
setup: Mix a few drops of food coloring into each spray bottle ahead of time.
steps: Head outside to clean, fresh snow.
Spray big shapes first: circles, zigzags, your initials.
Layer colors to make new ones where they overlap.
Work together on one giant mural across the snowbank.
Step back and admire it before it melts.
tagline: Spray colored water onto fresh snow and paint the whole yard.

variations.easier: Use one color and paint footprints.
variations.harder: Plan the mural on paper first, then spray it to scale.

materials.item: small mason jars or clear cups with lids

name: Snowman Soup Gift Mix
safety: Use only sealed, store-bought ingredients; check dairy and nut allergies. Wash hands before handling food.
setup: Open sealed bags into pouring bowls just before the activity; set out jars and tags.
steps: Spoon cocoa mix into the jar: about half full.
Layer chocolate chips, then mini marshmallows on top.
Seal the jar and tie ribbon around the lid.
Write the recipe tag: mix with hot water or warm milk.
Give it to someone who could use a warm-up.
tagline: Layer cocoa, marshmallows, and chocolate chips into a gift-ready jar.

variations.easier: Use one jar size and a printed tag to copy.
variations.harder: Design your own tag art and write a personal note.

materials.item: paper and pencils for the route plan
lanterns or jar candles (real walk) or drawings (planning only)
a printed map of the block or school grounds

name: Solstice Lantern Stroll
safety: Real flames stay with adults only; kids carry battery candles. Walk in a group with an adult leader and wear reflective gear.
setup: Print simple maps; confirm the walk route and adult helpers with the program lead first.
steps: Learn what the winter solstice is: the longest night of the year.
Draw a safe walking loop on the map: start, middle stop, finish.
Assign jobs: route leader, lantern carriers, song starter, caboose.
Make or decorate the lanterns.
Walk the loop together as the sky goes dark.
tagline: Plan a lantern walk for the longest night of the year.

variations.easier: Plan the walk and do a daytime practice loop instead.
variations.harder: Write the invitation and lead the whole event yourselves.

materials.item: bins labeled recycle, trash, and keep

name: Holiday Cleanup Crew Game
safety: Adults handle anything sharp or broken; kids sort paper and packaging only.
setup: Label the bins and place them where everyone can reach them.
steps: Split into crews: Wrappers, Recyclers, and Keepers.
Set the timer for ten minutes.
Sort everything into the right bin; one point per correct item.
Pause at five minutes: which crew is winning?
Final count. The winning crew picks the closing song.
tagline: Turn the post-party mess into a timed team mission.

variations.easier: Skip the points; just beat the timer together.
